name: Educational hot-flash risk indicator
trainedOn: TSHS Hot Flashes dataset (Freeman et al., 2001 baseline), n=375 women aged 35-48
citation: Grau L, Okungu X, Sammel MD. "Hot Flashes Dataset", TSHS Resources Portal (2023). https://www.causeweb.org/tshs/hot-flashes/
outcome: Self-reported hot flashes in the past month
caveat: Educational indicator from a small 2001 cohort of late-reproductive-age women; not a validated prediction for any individual.

evaluation.method: Repeated stratified 5-fold CV (20 repeats, seed 7); all models share the same folds. cvAucMean/Sd summarise the 100 per-fold AUCs. Out-of-fold (OOF) probabilities are averaged over the 20 repeats to give one held-out prediction per woman; oofAuc, calibration and fairness use these, with 95% CIs from 2000 bootstrap resamples of women (percentile method). Calibration slope/recalibration intercept come from regressing the outcome on logit(OOF probability); 'intercept' fixes the slope at 1 (calibration-in-the-large). Reliability table uses 5 equal-count bins.

base.rationale: Logistic regression out-of-fold AUC 0.702 (95% CI 0.643-0.757) vs gradient boosting 0.706 (0.650-0.761); paired difference -0.004 (95% CI -0.021 to +0.012). The interval includes zero, so the two are comparable and boosting gives no reliable gain. Logistic regression is kept because each factor maps to a readable odds ratio shown to the user, it runs as a few coefficients on-device, and it is less prone to overfitting 375 rows. Both beat the intercept-only baseline (per-fold AUC 0.50; its pooled OOF AUC sits slightly below 0.5 because each held-out fold's prevalence is anti-correlated with the training-fold prevalence it is given).

withLabs.rationale: Logistic regression out-of-fold AUC 0.749 (95% CI 0.695-0.798) vs gradient boosting 0.714 (0.653-0.770); paired difference +0.035 (95% CI +0.012 to +0.057). Logistic regression is reliably better here; boosting appears to overfit the small sample. Logistic regression is kept because each factor maps to a readable odds ratio shown to the user, it runs as a few coefficients on-device, and it is less prone to overfitting 375 rows. Both beat the intercept-only baseline (per-fold AUC 0.50; its pooled OOF AUC sits slightly below 0.5 because each held-out fold's prevalence is anti-correlated with the training-fold prevalence it is given).

base.note: Race and education are not model inputs; they are used only to audit out-of-fold logistic-regression predictions. Metrics are suppressed (null) when a group has n<30 or fewer than 10 events/non-events.

race.finding: By race, out-of-fold AUC was African American 0.69 (95% CI 0.61-0.77, n=182); Caucasian 0.65 (95% CI 0.55-0.75, n=193). The intervals overlap, so this sample cannot show a reliable difference in ranking performance (it also cannot rule one out). Observed hot-flash prevalence ranged from 25% (Caucasian) to 38% (African American). Average predicted and observed rates agree within sampling error for every reported group.
race.summary: AUC 0.69 (African American) vs 0.65 (Caucasian); intervals overlap, no reliable gap detected at this sample size; predicted rates match observed rates in each group.

education.finding: By education, out-of-fold AUC was High school or more 0.69 (95% CI 0.63-0.76, n=336); Less than high school 0.57 (95% CI 0.38-0.75, n=39). The intervals overlap, so this sample cannot show a reliable difference in ranking performance (it also cannot rule one out). Observed hot-flash prevalence ranged from 29% (High school or more) to 51% (Less than high school). For Less than high school the AUC interval includes 0.5, so better-than-chance ranking is not established for that group. Average predicted and observed rates agree within sampling error for every reported group.
